text:
Two years after Jasper National Park went up in flames, a majority of attractions have reopened.

That includes all of the backcountry campsites and 77 per cent of frontcountry campsites.

"The regrowth through the wildfire impacted areas has been really amazing,” said Amy Cairns, Director of Recovery for Jasper National Park. “Right now, the grass is super high and there's lots of wildflowers everywhere.”

How far along is the Jasper rebuild?

Parks Canada data shows visitation in the area is rebounding. Visitation numbers for this year match last year’s numbers and are within five per cent of 2023 pre-fire levels, the agency's data shows.

Additionally, frontcountry camping reservations for July and August remain near capacity.

To encourage travel, national park admission is free until Sept. 7 and camping fees are discounted by 25 per cent, through the Canada Strong Pass.

Among open attractions are all of the backcountry campsites and a majority of frontcountry campsites, including 80 newly reopened sites at the Whistlers and Wapiti campgrounds.

But, in some areas where trees provided coverage between sites and roadways, some fire-affected areas are more exposed.

Alberta rejects federal nature strategy, redefines protected land

Earlier this summer, Parks Canada reopened Wabasso Lake, the Curator Trail and the Valley of the Five Lakes Trail.

Parks Canada addressed trail erosion and invasive plants on the popular Valley of the Five Lakes Trail, a scenic five-kilometre loop around glacial lakes, Cairns said, adding the agency rerouted the trail onto some ridges for “spectacular views” and added stonework for new stairs.

The two major attractions still off-limits are the Edith Cavell Area and Maligne Canyon.

Cavell Road remains closed to all vehicles and hikers due to ongoing slope instability and the ongoing risks of landslides and rockfalls. The road leads to popular hiking routes, including the Path of the Glacier and Cavell Meadows trails at Mount Edith Cavell, which are also closed.

Further north, Maligne Canyon, including its day-use area and trail, remains closed. Recovery teams are working through detailed engineering plans to address geotechnical concerns and danger trees along the canyon's steep drop-offs before guided tours and visitors can safely return.

Short-term rentals up for debate in Hinton as mountain town balances tourism demand with housing

As for accommodations, 23 per cent of frontcountry campsites still remain closed. All of Wabasso, Whirlpool Group and Marmot Meadows Group campgrounds remain closed for full infrastructure rebuilds.

A portion of Wapiti Campground is also closed.

Additionally, Trail 9C — a trail connecting Old Fort Point Trail to the Valley of the Five Lakes Trail — is still shuttered for hazard tree removal.

Last month, Ottawa announced a $520-million injection into the rebuild efforts following the 2024 Jasper Wildfire.

The funds will be allocated to repairing Parks Canada infrastructure, wildfire risk reduction, expediting permitting and continuing interim housing through March 2028, Cairns said.

Parks Canada is prioritizing road work this summer and into the winter, she added.

Before the Marmot Basin ski area can be ready for the winter season, slope flattening and improving drainage on Mile 5 Hill will begin this fall to address stability and rockfall from the springtime.

Jasper to get $520M in additional reconstruction funding from federal government

Work in the Mount Edith Cavell area will begin by the end of the summer to repave and establish retaining walls to address slope stability.

While the 2024 wildfire only burned three per cent of Jasper National Park, 20 per cent of Park infrastructure was damaged or destroyed.

Now, Parks Canada's priority is to get everything that is still closed back open to the public safely, Cairns said.

“It's just a neat experience to walk through those [fire affected] areas and see regeneration and regrowth in action.”

Reporter

Maggie Kirk is a reporter for CBC News in Hinton, Alta.
